scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Inscribed by UNESCO in 2008, the Makishi masquerade brings ancestral spirits to the village as boys emerge from months of isolation in a secret bush camp.
This is Makishi masquerade. Traditional, pre-colonial; UNESCO proclaimed 2005/2008.
on_screen: Title card: Makishi masquerade · Zambia · Traditional, pre-colonial; UNESCO proclaimed 2005/2008

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Makishi masquerade originates in the pre-colonial traditions of the Vaka Chiyama Cha Mukwamayi communities of northwestern and western Zambia.
It forms an integral part of the mukanda initiation cycle shared by the Luvale, Chokwe, Luchazi, and Mbunda peoples.

Due to threats to its continuity from modern socio-economic changes and shifting religious practices, the masquerade was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity and inscribed by UNESCO in 2008.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The masquerade marks the celebratory conclusion of the mukanda initiation ritual for boys, symbolizing their transition from childhood death to rebirth as adult men equipped with community values and survival knowledge.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Masks and costumes represent deceased ancestors and various archetypes, featuring horns, points, trompes, and crests constructed during the bush camp period.
The ritual is set across isolated bush camps, cemeteries where men seek ancestral possession, and the village public spaces where the final graduation and pantomime take place.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key characters include Chisaluke representing a wealthy and powerful man, Mupala as the lord and protector of the mukanda, Pwevo as the ideal woman, and Chilea as the dance trainer.
Celebrated across the northwestern and western provinces of Zambia by the Luvale, Chokwe, Luchazi, and Mbunda peoples belonging to the Vaka Chiyama Cha Mukwamayi communities.
Linked broadly to southern savanna initiation rites and masking traditions extending across Central Africa from Angola through the Democratic Republic of Congo into Zambia.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The Makishi masquerade is tied to sacred mukanda initiation rites, where participants spend time in isolated bush camps and men spend the night before the ritual at the cemetery to be possessed by ancestors; outsiders must respect these sacred boundaries.
